name: Average cost and realised P&L
brief:
A position in one share keeps its average cost. A buy of `qty` at `price` blends into the average. A sell realises `qty * (price - avg_cost)` and leaves the average alone; once the position is flat, the average goes back to `0.0`. The position is never short: a sell of more than is held raises `ValueError`, and so does a `qty` that is not above zero. A refused trade changes nothing.

Write the class `CostBasis` with attributes `qty` (an `int`), `avg_cost` and `realised` (both start at 0), and methods `buy(qty, price)`, `sell(qty, price)` and `unrealised(price)`, which is `qty * (price - avg_cost)`.

Example. Buy 100 at £4.00 and 300 at £4.40: the cost is £1,720 for 400 shares, an average of £4.30. Sell 200 at £4.50: £40 is realised, and 200 shares remain at £4.30.
constraints: Quantities are whole numbers; prices are £ floats.
Numbers are compared with `math.isclose` at a relative tolerance of $10^{-9}$.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Check a trade before you change anything. On a buy the new average is (old shares times old average plus the new cost) over the new shares.

examples.call: (c := CostBasis(), c.buy(100, 4.00), c.buy(300, 4.40), c.sell(200, 4.50), (c.qty, c.avg_cost, c.realised))[-1]
examples.note: The average is £1,720 over 400 shares. The sale realises 200 times 20p.
Only 10 shares are held, so a sell of 11 is refused.

tests.call: (c := CostBasis(), c.buy(100, 4.00), c.buy(300, 4.40), c.sell(200, 4.50), (c.qty, c.avg_cost, c.realised))[-1]
(c := CostBasis(), c.buy(100, 4.0), c.sell(100, 5.0), c.buy(50, 6.0), (c.qty, c.avg_cost, c.realised))[-1]
(c := CostBasis(), c.buy(30, 10.0), c.sell(10, 12.0), c.sell(10, 9.0), (c.qty, c.avg_cost, c.realised))[-1]

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. A number is accepted when `math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9)` holds, element by element for lists and tuples; anything else must equal the expected value. In a test, `_raised(f)` calls `f` and gives the name of the error it raises, or `'no error'`.
notes: The object keeps three numbers that must agree, and each method checks a trade before it changes any of them.
Keeping a running total cost and dividing it after a sell moves the average, which a sell must not do.
Every method does a fixed amount of work, so each trade is $O(1)$.

planted.slip: The total cost is never reduced on a sell, so the average jumps after every sale.
It changes the position first and checks after, so a refused sell still moves the numbers.
The old average stays after the position is sold out.
